film: SC-238 · the landing film v3, Twenty-Two Days
opening: Near-expiry stock, routed by AI agents. One yes from a person.

lines.text: The distributor: “Twenty-two days left on the mango.”
The supply chain lead: “And quick commerce?”
The distributor: “They won't take it.”
The supply chain lead: “Write it off, then.”
Every morning in India, good food runs out of time.
Not spoiled. Just short on days.
India's food regulator says packaged food sold online must reach your door with at least thirty per cent of its shelf life, or forty-five days, still left.
And the quick-commerce apps usually ask for far more: about sixty per cent of the shelf life, or ninety days and up.
This batch has twenty-two days. It is below every line.
If it is written off, the brand loses the stock, reverses its tax credit and pays to destroy it: twenty-two thousand rupees, on one batch.
Week after week. Brand after brand.
What if every one of those packs could still find a home?
This is Smart-Clearance: agentic software that turns write-offs into recovery.
Every brand gets its own workspace, set up from one console in minutes: its stock data, its distributors, its people and its own rules.
From the console, the platform team watches every client, every agent and every batch, live.
Each team sees its own part, the brand, the distributors, the kiranas and the food banks, installed on any phone, tablet or laptop.
No app store needed: it installs straight from the browser, and every alert arrives as a notification.
Inside every workspace works a team that never sleeps.
Ten agents. Nine think with Gemini, on Google's Agent Platform. The Watcher runs on plain rules.
The Data agent reads each distributor's stock export.
Every morning, the Watcher checks each batch's sell-through against the apps' gates.
Vision reads the label from one photo.
The Valuer prices every exit, the bin included.
The Router splits the batch where it earns the most.
Then it stops, at a person. Nothing moves without one yes.
Outreach takes the offer to the kiranas. The Lister and the Negotiator work a marketplace, when a batch has the days.
Paperwork draws every paper.
And Impact counts the good it does.
And all of it runs on the brand's own rules, for dates, prices and credit. The models never touch the money.
At nine, the Watcher flags a mango drink: fifteen hundred and eighty packs that won't sell in time.
The distributor sends one photo. Vision checks the label against the stock.
By nine twenty, the plan is priced: the kiranas, a staff sale and a food bank, and nothing to the bin.
The brand's head: “Nothing to the bin?”
The supply chain lead: “Not one pack. Approved.”
One tap, and the agents go to work.
Outreach sends the distributor's kiranas the offer, in Hindi.
A kirana owner: “Two free with every ten!”
Each order lands with its own GST invoice.
A food bank volunteer: “Fifty-eight packs. All sealed.”
A food bank collects what is closest to its date, with its own receipt.
The next day, the staff buy their share by UPI, and Vision checks the receipt against the count.
A shopkeeper: “The bill's inside? Good.”
Instead of a twenty-two-thousand-rupee loss, nearly seventeen thousand recovered, and the distributor ends whole.
The distributor sees it all on her own portal: every order, every paper and every rupee credited.
Not every batch is that easy. In Nagpur, a batch of chips is split two ways: a lot on a near-expiry marketplace, and a scheme for the kiranas.
The Negotiator closes the lot at fourteen rupees twenty a pack, without ever showing the floor price.
A wholesale buyer: “Fourteen-twenty. Done. Truck's coming.”
But only two shops order. When the window closes, five hundred and forty packets are left.
On expiry day, an authorised agency destroys them, and the distributor records it on his tablet: the packs slit open, buried, and covered.
The photos go up, and
the certificate is signed on the spot: by the agency’s officer, two witnesses, and the distributor.
The distributor, at the landfill: “All four signatures. It’s on record.”
He sends it, and
Vision checks both photos against the batch and the slate.
And nothing is credited for them until a second yes.
Only then are the expiry credit note and the certificate issued, and the distributor is made whole.
Every paper is drawn, signed where it must be, and reviewed: GST invoices and e-invoices, credit notes, the tax-credit memo, receipts and certificates.
And every step is on the record: which agent did what, who said yes, and when.
Every rupee adds up against what the bin would have cost, and every batch posts to an impact ledger, ready for the brand's sustainability report.
On the mango alone: three hundred and forty kilos kept out of landfill, and fifty-eight meals.
The distributor: “Every credit note arrived on time.”
The supply chain lead: “Not one pack went to waste.”
Smart-Clearance. Ten agents. One yes. And nothing good goes to waste.
